zone: Flat Creek and the upper Stehekin valley
_areas_note: Rimrock Ridge alone. THE GROUPING WAS CHECKED AGAINST THE GROUND RATHER THAN TAKEN ON TRUST, and the ridge turns out to be a watershed divide: its north side drains into Flat Creek and its south side into the West Fork of Agnes Creek, with the summit line sitting exactly on the boundary. The Flat Creek side is the approach — a long walk up a closed road and then a maintained valley trail — and that is why this file exists. NOT added to either Ptarmigan crest file: the ridge stands a couple of miles east of the crest and those camps serve summits above the glaciers on its far side. NOT added to the existing Stehekin file either, and that one needed checking: its West Fork Agnes bivy is in the same named drainage as this peak's south side, but sits more than ten kilometres east under Agnes Mountain up a drainage whose trail has all but vanished, so it is not a base for this summit. The landing camps and the shuttle terminus at High Bridge are recorded there and are NOT duplicated here though every party passes through both; Bridge Creek camps are left out because a neighbouring file holds them, and the Park Creek camp below is the one ON THE VALLEY ROAD, not the Five Mile stock camp further up the Park Creek trail that another file already carries. THE OBVIOUS CAMP FOR THIS PEAK IS SHUT: Flat Creek Camp, at the trailhead itself, is closed for hazard trees on its access trail and appears in neither the park's current camp table nor its reservation inventory, so it is deliberately NOT listed as a site here. The park's own stated substitute is Park Creek. NO ELEVATIONS ARE RECORDED for any camp in this file because the park publishes none for them anywhere, and the figures circulating elsewhere are second-hand.

sites.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
sites.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.
sites.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. THERE IS NO PERMIT DESK IN STEHEKIN — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by EMAIL with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning BEFORE your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
sites.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.

sites.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
sites.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. WALK-UP ONLY — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.
sites.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
sites.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to BICYCLES as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.

sites.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
sites.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.
sites.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A TOTAL CAMPFIRE BAN has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane STOVES are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
sites.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP THE PARK ITSELF POINTS OVERNIGHT PARTIES TO NOW THAT FLAT CREEK IS SHUT, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the VALLEY ROAD where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.

sites.name: Cottonwood Camp, end of the closed road
sites.capacity: Two sites, one taking six and one taking twelve, so up to twelve in a party — the largest allowance anywhere on this approach and the reason groups use it.
sites.water: River and tributary water at the camp, reliable and needing treatment like everything else in the drainage.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. WHICH OFFICE DEPENDS ON WHICH WAY YOU COME IN, and getting this wrong costs a day: a party arriving by boat arranges it by email with the wilderness office before travelling, but anyone approaching over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road must collect the permit IN PERSON at Marblemount, and that includes permits for this camp. The camp table allows campfires here, but the valley-wide ban currently overrides that.
sites.notes: At the very end of the closed road section, something under four miles past the Flat Creek junction, roughly twenty-three miles up from the landing. It is the upper valley's anchor camp and the obvious base for a larger party, at the cost of walking past your turning and back each day. It also marks where the OTHER approaches arrive: parties come down over Park Creek Pass from the Thunder Creek side, and over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road, which reaches the Flat Creek junction in something over thirteen miles. Either is a genuine alternative to the boat and both are long. Worth knowing that the current fire closures in this park are all on the Ross Lake and Big Beaver side and do NOT reach the upper Stehekin valley — the camps up here are constrained by flood damage, hazard trees and the fire ban, not by an active fire.

sites.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
sites.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.
sites.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
sites.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of TWELVE counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
sites.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
